bloques.texto:
On April 18, 2018, a 72-year-old man parks outside a craft store in Roseville, California.

He goes inside to shop. While he's gone, a detective walks up to his car and quietly swabs the door handle.

He has no idea.

For more than forty years, police had been hunting one man. At least thirteen murders. Around fifty sexual assaults. More than a hundred burglaries. Across California.

This is the case of the Golden State Killer. Part one.

Most people think serial killers get caught because they make a mistake.

But here's what makes this case so disturbing.

For over a decade, this man attacked again and again, and he almost never made a mistake. He wore a mask. He wore gloves. He studied his victims for weeks. He knew how police worked.

And there was a reason he knew.

So the real question isn't how he was caught.

It's this. How did one man terrorise an entire state for twelve years… and then simply disappear into a normal life for three more decades?

The story starts in 1974, in a quiet farming town called Visalia, in California's Central Valley.

Houses were being broken into. Dozens of them. Then more than a hundred.

But the burglar was strange. He rarely took anything valuable. He went through drawers. He scattered underwear and photographs. He took small, personal things. Coins. Rings. Pictures.

Police called him the Visalia Ransacker.

Then, in September 1975, it turned violent. A man tried to take a teenage girl from her home. Her father, a journalism professor named Claude Snelling, ran outside to stop him.

The intruder shot him. Claude Snelling died. His daughter survived.

Police set traps. In December 1975, a Visalia detective named Bill McGowen staked out a house the Ransacker had targeted before.

That night, a masked man appeared in the backyard. McGowen shouted at him to stop. The man raised his hands, as if to surrender.

Then he pulled a gun and fired. The bullet struck McGowen's flashlight. The flashlight saved his life.

The man escaped over a fence.

After that, the Ransacker vanished.

And just a few miles away, in the small town of Exeter, a young police officer was working burglaries.

His name was Joseph James DeAngelo.

DeAngelo was born in 1945 in New York. He served in the Navy during the Vietnam War. He studied criminal justice. In 1973, he became a police officer in Exeter.

In 1976, he moved north, to the town of Auburn, near Sacramento. He married. He had a badge, a uniform and a gun.

And that same year, in the suburbs east of Sacramento, something new began.

In June 1976, a man in a mask broke into a home at night and attacked a young woman.

Then another. And another.

The newspapers called him the East Area Rapist.

Over the next three years, he attacked around fifty people in and around Sacramento.

He had a pattern, and police learned it the hard way.

He prowled neighbourhoods for weeks before an attack. He studied the homes. Some victims later remembered strange phone calls. Someone breathing on the line. Then silence.

He came at night, through a window or a sliding door. He wore a ski mask. He spoke in a whisper, through clenched teeth.

And when the victim was a couple, he did something that terrified the whole city. He tied them up and made one partner believe that if they moved, the other would die.

Then he took his time. He ate food from their kitchen. He went through their drawers. Sometimes he stayed for hours.

He took small things. Coins. Rings. Driver's licences. Things that meant nothing to anyone but the victims.

And then he was gone. Into the night. On foot, or on a bicycle.

Police dogs lost his trail again and again. Composite sketches went to every newspaper. Hundreds of men were questioned.

None of them was him.

By 1977, Sacramento was afraid.

People bought guns and guard dogs. They put locks on every window. Hardware stores ran out of deadbolts. Neighbours organised night patrols.

Police held public meetings. At one of them, a man stood up and said the attacker would never dare to strike a home with a man inside.

Weeks later, the East Area Rapist attacked a couple.

Investigators also noticed something unsettling. He seemed to know police tactics. When they set up stakeouts in one area, he struck in another. When they changed patrol routes, he changed too.

Some detectives quietly wondered if he could be one of them.

A task force was formed. Detectives worked through the night. Some of them would spend the rest of their careers on this case.

Nobody looked at an officer in the small town of Auburn.

On the evening of February 2, 1978, a young couple, Brian and Katie Maggiore, were walking their dog in Rancho Cordova, a suburb of Sacramento.

They saw something. Maybe a man prowling. Maybe they surprised him.

The man chased them and shot them both. Brian and Katie Maggiore died.

Witnesses saw a man running from the scene. Police drew a sketch.

It didn't lead anywhere.

The East Area Rapist was now a killer.

bloques.titulo: The hammer and the dog repellent
bloques.texto:
Then, in July 1979, something small happened.

An off-duty police officer from Auburn was caught at a store in Citrus Heights trying to steal two items. A hammer. And a can of dog repellent.

He was Joseph James DeAngelo.

Auburn fired him in August 1979. It looked like a minor scandal. An embarrassing end to a short police career.

Nobody connected it to the East Area Rapist.

But think about those two items. A tool. And something to stop dogs from barking.

That same year, the attacks in Sacramento stopped.

Around the same time, the violence moved south, hundreds of miles away, to the coast of Southern California.

In October 1979, in Goleta, near Santa Barbara, a couple was attacked in their home at night. They managed to escape and scream for help. The intruder fled.

Two months later, in Goleta, he came back. On December 30, 1979, Dr. Robert Offerman and Debra Manning were killed.

In March 1980, in Ventura, Lyman and Charlene Smith were killed.

In August 1980, in Dana Point, newlyweds Keith and Patrice Harrington were killed.

In February 1981, in Irvine, Manuela Witthuhn was killed.

In July 1981, back in Goleta, Cheri Domingo and Gregory Sanchez were killed.

Police in Southern California called him the Original Night Stalker.

In Sacramento, they called him the East Area Rapist.

Nobody yet knew it was the same man.

Then, nothing. For almost five years.

Until May 4, 1986. In Irvine, an 18-year-old named Janelle Cruz was killed while her family was on holiday.

She was the last known victim.

After that, he stopped. Completely.

No more attacks. No more calls. The man in the mask simply disappeared.

And Joseph James DeAngelo? By then, he was working as a mechanic at a supermarket warehouse near Sacramento. He had three daughters. He lived in a quiet house in Citrus Heights.

He mowed his lawn. He fixed his car. His neighbours knew him as a grumpy man who swore at the dog next door.

He would keep that life for thirty-two years.

Through the 1980s and 1990s, the files sat in boxes in different police departments. Different counties. Different names for the same man.

Then DNA testing arrived.

In 2001, crime labs compared DNA from the East Area Rapist cases with DNA from the Original Night Stalker murders.

It matched.

One man was responsible for all of it.

Now police had his genetic fingerprint. But it matched no one in any criminal database. Whoever he was, he had never been arrested for anything that put his DNA on file.

Investigators kept working. In 2016, the FBI announced a fifty-thousand-dollar reward and released new details: the type of shoes he wore, his possible height, a drawing of a map he may have left behind.

Tips came in by the thousands.

None of them led to him.

The killer had a DNA profile. He still had no name.

Years later, a true crime writer named Michelle McNamara became obsessed with the case.

She gave him the name that stuck: the Golden State Killer.

She spent years reading files, interviewing detectives and building timelines. She believed he was still alive. Still out there. Living somewhere in plain sight.

She died in 2016, before she could finish her book.

Her words were published two months before the man she was hunting was found.

And the detectives working the case had one last idea. A strange, new, controversial idea.

DNA was everywhere now. Not just in police labs. Millions of ordinary people were spitting into tubes and mailing them to companies, just to learn where their ancestors came from.

What if the killer wasn't in any police database… but his relatives were in a family tree?

How do you find a man with no name, using the DNA of people he's never met?

That's in Part 2.

shorts.texto:
Let me tell you about the most important car door handle in California history.

April 18, 2018. A 72-year-old man goes shopping at a craft store.

While he's inside, a detective walks up to his car.

And swabs the handle.

He has no idea who's been looking for him. Or for how long.

Forty-two years.

Thirteen murders. Around fifty attacks. And police were about to learn his name.

But to understand how, we have to go back to 1976.

Part two.

Imagine the man terrorising your city is wearing a police badge.

Sacramento, 1976. A masked man breaks into homes at night.

He studies neighbourhoods for weeks. He knows how police think.

When police watch one area, he strikes another.

Some detectives quietly wonder if he's one of them.

Nobody looks at a young officer in the small town of Auburn.

In 1979, that officer is caught stealing a hammer… and dog repellent.

And then the attacks in Sacramento stop.

Part three.

Here's what scared investigators most. In 1986, he just stopped.

No more attacks. No more calls. Nothing.

By then, he'd moved his violence south. Goleta. Ventura. Dana Point. Irvine.

Then, after one last murder in May 1986, he vanished.

Not into prison. Into a normal life.

A mechanic. A father. A man who mowed his lawn in Citrus Heights.

For thirty-two years.

Police had his DNA. They just didn't have his name.

Part four.
